content: Calcium citrate is the calcium salt derived from citric acid. It is frequently utilized as a food additive, identified as E333, primarily serving as a preservative, though it is occasionally employed to enhance flavor. In this regard, it shares similarities with sodium citrate. Additionally, calcium citrate functions as a water softener due to the ability of citrate ions to chelate and bind with undesirable metal ions. It is also a component in certain dietary calcium supplements. Calcium citrate possesses a sour taste, akin to citric acid. However, like other salts, it also exhibits a salty flavor. This combination of sour and salty characteristics has led to citrates, such as sodium citrate and calcium citrate, being commonly referred to as sour salt. The production of calcium citrate involves its role as an intermediate in the industrial extraction of citric acid through fermentation processes. During this process, citric acid present in the fermentation broth is neutralized using calcium hydroxide, resulting in the precipitation of insoluble calcium citrate. This precipitate is subsequently separated from the broth through filtration and thoroughly washed to yield purified calcium citrate. The resulting calcium citrate can either be marketed in its current form or further processed into citric acid by reacting it with dilute sulfuric acid. Calcium citrate supplements have been associated with an increased risk of aluminum toxicity, particularly in patients with renal disease, who are more susceptible to such toxicity. The bioavailability of calcium citrate is approximately 2.5 times greater than that of calcium carbonate. Consequently, individuals who have undergone Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery, a type of weight-loss procedure, are typically advised to use calcium citrate as their preferred form of dietary calcium supplementation.
